title: At the café
goal: Order food and drink politely, and take on the pattern that trips up beginners more than any other: consonants that weaken when a word changes form.
bekal: order with *saisinko*, *otan*, and *haluaisin* — three levels of politeness
recognize the weakening of **k, p, t** and apply it yourself to new words
name thirty foods and drinks you will actually find in a Finnish café

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Kahvilassa Kampissa
dialogs.intro: After class, Budi and Aino stop at a café in the Kamppi shopping center in Helsinki.

lines.speaker: Aino:
lines.text: Tässä kahvilassa on hyvät pullat. Mitä sinä otat?
lines.id: The sweet buns in this café are good. What are you having?
lines.literal: in-this in-café is good-plural bun-plural. what you take?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: En tiedä vielä. Mikä tuo on?
lines.id: I don't know yet. What's that?
lines.literal: not-I know still. what that-there is?

lines.speaker: Aino:
lines.text: Se on korvapuusti. Se on kanelipulla.
lines.id: That's a korvapuusti. A cinnamon bun.
lines.literal: it is korvapuusti. it is cinnamon-bun.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Great. I'll take that and a coffee.

lines.speaker: Myyjä:
lines.id: Hi! What can I get you?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Saisinko yhden korvapuustin ja yhden kahvin?
lines.id: Could I have one korvapuusti and one coffee?
lines.literal: may-I-get one-'s korvapuusti-'s and one-'s coffee-'s?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Maidon kanssa, kiitos. Onko teillä teetä?
lines.id: With milk, thanks. Do you have tea?
lines.literal: milk-'s with, thanks. is-? at-you tea-some?

lines.speaker: Myyjä:
lines.text: On. Vihreää teetä ja mustaa teetä.
lines.id: Yes. Green tea and black tea.
lines.literal: is. green-some tea-some and black-some tea-some.

lines.speaker: Aino:
lines.text: Minä otan vihreän teen ja yhden voileivän.
lines.id: I'll have a green tea and a sandwich.
lines.literal: I take green-'s tea-'s and one-'s sandwich-'s.

lines.speaker: Myyjä:
lines.text: Kaksitoista euroa yhteensä. Tässä tai mukaan?
lines.id: Twelve euros altogether. For here or to go?
lines.literal: twelve euro-some together. in-this or along?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Tässä, kiitos. Onko täällä vapaa pöytä?
lines.id: For here, thanks. Is there a free table?
lines.literal: in-this, thanks. is-? here free table?

lines.speaker: Myyjä:
lines.id: Yes, by the window. Here you go!

notes: **Kahvila → kahvilassa, but kauppa → kaupassa.** Compare two words from this unit: one stays the same, the other loses a *p*. The difference is simple — *kahvila* has no *k*, *p*, or *t* in its last syllable, so there is nothing to weaken. The full rule is in the next box.

**Saisinko** literally means "may-I would get" — the conditional form of *saada* (to get) plus the question ending. It is the politest and most common way to order anywhere in Finland. You don't need to understand the form yet; learn it whole and use it every day.

**What you order takes the genitive.** *Otan kahvi**n***, *saisinko yhde**n** korvapuusti**n***. The *-n* here doesn't mean possession; it marks that the thing is **taken in full** — one whole coffee, not some of it. Compare *otan kahvi**a*** (I'll take some coffee = coffee with no set amount). This rule is covered fully in Unit 11.

**Teetä, vihreää teetä.** After *onko teillä*, the item takes the partitive because the amount isn't fixed. Note that **the adjective follows suit**: *vihreä teetä* becomes *vihreä**ä** teetä*. Once again, the adjective always copies the form of its noun.

**Ikkunan vieressä** — "by the window". Words like *vieressä* (beside), *edessä* (in front of), *takana* (behind) always come **after** their noun, and the noun takes the genitive. English puts them before; Finnish turns it around.
**Mitä saisi olla?** literally "what may be" — the standard phrase of café and shop staff. Its cousin: *Kuinka voin auttaa?* (how can I help).

grammars.title: Consonant gradation — astevaihtelu
body: This is the pattern that most often makes beginners feel Finnish words "change however they like". In fact it is very regular, and the rule fits in one sentence: **when an ending closes the last syllable, the k/p/t in front of it weakens.**
after: **Words without k/p/t don't change at all.** *Kahvila → kahvilassa*, *talo → talossa*, *Espoo → Espoossa*. Most words actually fall into this group, so don't picture the whole of Finnish shifting under your feet.
⚠️ Only the k/p/t in the **last syllable** changes, not anywhere in the word. *Kahvi → kahvin* loses nothing because *v* isn't k/p/t; *tietokone → tietokoneen* is safe too.
For some words it runs the other way: a weak base turns strong when the ending arrives — *hake**a** → ha**k**een*, *sata → sadan* but *kaksi**sataa***. This group is smaller; don't chase it yet.

grammars.title: Three ways to order
body: Finnish has a clear politeness ladder for ordering, and all the rungs are used every day. What can go wrong isn't the grammar but the tone.
after: ⚠️ *Kiitos* at the end of the sentence isn't just a courtesy — it is what **makes** a short sentence polite. *Yksi kahvi* without *kiitos* sounds like a command; with *kiitos*, it is perfectly normal.
If you're asked *Mitä saisi olla?* and you're not ready, say *Hetkinen* (just a moment) or *Anteeksi, minä mietin vielä* (sorry, I'm still thinking). Nobody is in a hurry.
Paying: *Kortilla vai käteisellä?* (card or cash?). The answer is almost always *Kortilla* — Finland has almost entirely given up cash, and many small cafés don't accept it at all.

blocks.text: The third column is there on purpose: it is the form you use when ordering (*otan kahvi**n***), and it also shows whether the consonant weakens. Look at *maito → maido**n***, *leipä → leivä**n***, *olut → olue**n***.

blocks.title: Four sentences for people who don't eat just anything
items: *En syö sianlihaa.* — I don't eat pork. (*sianliha* = pork)
*Onko tässä maitoa?* — Is there milk in this?
*Olen allerginen pähkinöille.* — I'm allergic to nuts.

blocks.text: Finnish puts some place words **after** the noun, and the noun must take the genitive (*-n*). The order is the reverse of English prepositions, so it takes conscious practice.
Notice that almost all of them carry an ending you already know: *viere**ssä*** (in the side), *ede**ssä***, *väli**ssä***. Once you see the pattern, the list stops feeling like random memorization.

⚠️ *Lähellä* and *kaukana* want different endings on the noun: *aseman lähellä* (genitive) but *keskusta**sta** kaukana* (from). If in doubt, rephrase: *Asema on lähellä* (the station is near) is always safe.

exercises.prompt: Add the ending -ssa/-ssä. Watch the consonant gradation.
Change to the -n form (the form used when ordering).
Put the words in the right order.
